t: Wise elders, or a wise overseer?
p: Lightfoot follows the Armenian and the long recension: the elders defer 'to him as to one wise in God'.

readings.w: Lake's text (G L)
readings.en: but as wise (people) in God

readings.w: The Armenian (A) and the long recension (g), followed by Lightfoot (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: but as to one wise in God
readings.plain: Treating him as one wise in God

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the Greek manuscript. Lake grants that Lightfoot's reading 'certainly gives a better sense, but for that reason may be a correction': a copyist is more likely to smooth the text than to roughen it.
b: With Lightfoot's reading it is the young overseer who is wise in God; with Lake's it is the elders, who show their wisdom by deferring to him.

p: The Greek manuscript and the Latin have 'us'; the Armenian and the long recension 'you'.

readings.w: Lake's text (G L)
readings.en: who willed us

readings.w: The Armenian (A) and the long recension (g) (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: who willed you

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The two words differ by one letter in Greek. The sense is close either way: God, who willed and called his people.

t: 'In the place of God' or 'as a type of God'?
p: Greek topon, 'place', in the Greek manuscript, Latin and long recension; typon, 'type', in the Syriac and Armenian, preferred by Lightfoot.

readings.w: Lake's text (G L g)
readings.en: into the place of God

readings.w: The Syriac (S) and Armenian (A), followed by Lightfoot and Zahn (Lake's footnote; Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: as a type of God

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake: 'Lightfoot prefers τύπον, but it seems to be more probably a softening of the rather startling τόπον by the Syriac translator.' The harder reading is the more likely to be original.
b:
The two Greek words differ by one letter. The same choice comes again in the next phrase: the elders 'in the place of' (or 'as a type of') the council of the apostles. Lake: 'Cf. Trall. iii', where he prints 'the overseer, who is a type of the Father' (Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1). There too the witnesses differ: in Lightfoot's apparatus the Greek manuscript and the Latin read huion, 'son', which he calls corrupt and replaces with typon, the reading of the Syriac and the long recension, loosely paraphrased in the Armenian.

Lightfoot gives his reasons for typon: the Syriac word 'would naturally stand for τύπος, not for τόπος'; the parallel in To the Trallians 3:1; and a later church order, the Apostolic Constitutions (2.26), which he calls 'obviously moulded after Ignatius' and which has eis typon several times: 'the deaconess (hē diakonos) is to be honored by you as a type of the Holy Spirit', 'the presbyters ... as a type of us the apostles'. Catholic teaching cites this verse beside Trallians 3:1 for the bishop as 'like the living image of God the Father' (Catechism 1549).

t: The council of the apostles, or of the angels?
p: The Syriac reads 'the council of angels'; the Armenian 'as angels of a king'.

readings.w: Lake's text; the Greek manuscript, the Latin, the long recension and a quotation of Severus (G L g Sev-Syr, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: of the council of the apostles

readings.w: The Syriac (S, Lightfoot's Latin: angelorum consilii)
readings.en: of the council of angels

readings.w: The Armenian (A, Lightfoot's Latin: tanquam angeli regis)
readings.en: as (the) angels of a king

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and all the Greek witnesses. Lightfoot explains the Armenian as 'an erroneous rendering' of the Syriac word, 'which differently vocalized signifies rex or consilium', king or council.
b: With 'angels' the elders would stand for a heavenly court round God rather than for the apostles round Christ. No Greek witness has it.

a: The Lord was united with the Father
t: 'Being united': in the Greek and Latin only
p: The Syriac, the Armenian and the long recension do not have 'being united'.

readings.w: Lake's text; the Greek manuscript and the Latin (G L, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.orig: ἄνευ τοῦ πατρὸς οὐδὲν ἐποίησεν, ἡνωμένος ὤν
readings.en: did nothing without the Father, being united (with him)
readings.plain: The Lord was united with the Father

readings.w: The Syriac (S) and the Armenian (A), the long recension (g, in brackets in Lightfoot as a weaker witness here) and a quotation Lightfoot cites as Dam-Rup (Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: (the Lord) did nothing without the Father

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the Greek manuscript. Lightfoot prints the words in square brackets and compares Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:3, where Christ 'in spirit ... was united with the Father'.
b: Without the words, the Plain English Translation would read 'The Lord did nothing without the Father'.

t: 'Which is Jesus Christ' or 'There is one Jesus Christ'?
p: The Greek manuscript reads 'one' (heis), not 'which' (ho); Lightfoot conjectures 'who' (hos).

readings.w: Lake's text; the Latin (L, quod, referring to 'joy') and a quotation Lightfoot cites as Antioch (Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ χαρᾷ τῇ ἀμώμῳ, ὅ ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός
readings.en: in the blameless joy, which is Jesus Christ

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G, Lightfoot's apparatus); so Roberts and Donaldson's English
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ χαρᾷ τῇ ἀμώμῳ. εἷς ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός
readings.en: in the blameless joy. There is one Jesus Christ

readings.w: Lightfoot's conjecture, 'though there is no direct evidence in its favour'
readings.en: who (that is, this unity) is Jesus Christ
readings.plain: and this unity is Jesus Christ

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the Latin. Lightfoot calls the Greek manuscript's 'one' 'part of the confusion which extends over the following clauses in the existing Greek text'.
b: Lightfoot's reason for hos: it 'stands mid-way between the two extant readings' and explains both, and it matches 15:1, 'an unwavering spirit, which is Jesus Christ'. On his reading what 'is Jesus Christ' is the whole picture of unity, not the joy alone.

p: Lake prints 'Judaism' with the Latin; the Greek manuscript adds 'law', and the Armenian and the long recension read 'Jewish law'.

readings.w: Lake's text and Lightfoot's; the Latin (L, judaismum)
readings.en: we live according to Judaism

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: we live according to law, Judaism (Guy: 'according to Judaizing law')
readings.plain: living by the law of Judaism

readings.w: The Armenian (A, judaicam legem) and the long recension (g, in brackets in Lightfoot as a weaker witness here) (Lightfoot's apparatus); so Roberts and Donaldson's English
readings.en: we live according to Jewish law

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake, who prints the Latin's reading here without a footnote, as Lightfoot does.
b: 'Judaism' names a whole way of life, Paul's word in Galatians 1:13-14; 'Jewish law' narrows it to the law's rules. Fritz Guy quotes the verse in the Greek manuscript's form, 'according to Judaizing law', and reads it of 'an inner, spiritual attitude'.

a: his Word, who came forth from silence
p: The Greek manuscript and the Latin read 'his eternal Word, not coming forth from silence'. Lake and Lightfoot follow the Armenian and Severus.

readings.w: Lake's text: the Armenian (A) and a quotation in Severus of Antioch (Lake's footnote); Lightfoot and Zahn
readings.orig: ὅς ἐστιν αὐτοῦ λόγος ἀπὸ σιγῆς προελθών
readings.en: who is his Word, having come forth from silence
readings.plain: his Word, who came forth from silence

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G) and the Latin (L) (Lake's footnote)
readings.orig: ὅς ἐστιν αὐτοῦ λόγος ἀΐδιος οὐκ ἀπὸ σιγῆς προελθών
readings.en: who is his eternal Word, not having come forth from silence
readings.plain: his eternal Word, who did not come forth from silence

why: Lake prints the shorter reading, and says the longer one 'is rightly regarded by recent editors as a doctrinal emendation due to fear of Gnostic theories in which Σιγή and Θεός were the original pair from which Λόγος emanated'. A copyist was more likely to add 'eternal ... not' to guard against heresy than to take the words out.
b:
Lightfoot, who first argued for the reading in 1868, gives four reasons: it stands in 'the oldest extant form of the text', the Armenian, and in Severus, who comments on it ('This (statement) that He proceeded from silence means that He was ineffably begotten by the Father'); it suits the context ('made himself known'); it agrees with Ignatius's language of God's silence elsewhere (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1); and the insertion 'is much more easily explained than their omission'. He dates the change to the fourth or fifth century, when Marcellus of Ancyra was attacked by Eusebius for teaching, in words close to this verse, that the Word came forth after God's silence (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical Theology 2.9, as Lightfoot quotes it). Lake's footnote points to a passage of Clement of Alexandria; its reference is misread in both scans of his page, so it is not given here.

Read with the reading followed, the Word 'came forth from silence': God, silent until then, spoke. Read with the other, the Word is eternal and was never preceded by a silence. See the note on 'from silence' and the chapter page.

p: The one Greek manuscript adds 'life': 'living by the Lord's life'. Lake prints the text without it, as Lightfoot and Zahn do; the Latin and Armenian, as Lightfoot gives them, have no 'life'.

readings.w: Lake's text, with the Latin (L, secundum dominicam viventes) and the Armenian (A, 'the Lord's day, holy and first'); so Lightfoot and Zahn (Lightfoot's apparatus; Guy)
readings.en: but living according to the Lord's (day)

readings.w: The Greek Medicean manuscript (G) (Lightfoot's apparatus; Guy)
readings.en: but living according to the Lord's life (or: living a life according to the Lord's [day])

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake's printed text and supplies 'day' in brackets, the word Lightfoot understands (hēmeran). Lightfoot calls 'the correct reading ... unquestionably κατὰ κυριακὴν', and says the added word 'is condemned alike by the preponderance of authorities and by the following words', 'on which', which need a day. Lake prints the shorter text with no footnote on this word.
b:
Fritz Guy (Andrews University Seminary Studies, 1964) argues that zōēn 'should probably be retained': the Greek with it can be read as a cognate phrase, 'living a life according to the Lord's day', which is exactly what the Latin says; and older editions (Pearson and Smith, 1709; Hefele; Cureton) kept it. He concludes that the meaning stays 'ambiguous'. Lightfoot names Hilgenfeld as one who took the reading 'the Lord's life'.

With the reading followed, Ignatius sets the Sabbath beside 'the Lord's day'; with the other, beside 'the Lord's life', a way of living.

p: The witnesses differ on the little word: 'whom/which' (Lake), 'which thing' (the Latin), 'who' (the Greek manuscript).

readings.w: Lake's text, supported by the long recension's paraphrase (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: which (or whom) some deny

readings.w: The Latin (L) (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: which thing some deny

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G) (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: his death, who deny (it)
readings.plain: his death; there are those who deny it

why: Lake: 'g paraphrases but has ὅν not ὅ. A is ambiguous. There is thus a slight balance in favour of ὅν τινες.'
b: Greek hon can mean 'whom' (Christ) or 'which' (his death, masculine in Greek). Lake translates 'though some deny him'. Lightfoot takes it as 'his death': 'The allusion is to Docetism, which denied the reality of our Lord's passion', and compares Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 5:1, 'Some, not knowing him, deny him'. The Plain English Translation's 'which' follows the nearer noun, his death.

a: those who lived in the old ways
p: The long recension reads 'old writings' (grammasin) for 'old practices' (pragmasin).

readings.w: Lake's text; the Greek manuscript, the Latin and the Armenian (G L A, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: those who lived in old practices
readings.plain: those who lived in the old ways

readings.w: The long recension (g, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: those who lived in old writings
readings.plain: those who lived by the old writings

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the best witnesses. Lightfoot calls the long recension's reading 'tempting' (it recalls Romans 7:6, 'the old letter') but rejects it: 'The convergence of the best authorities is decidedly in favour of πράγμασιν', and 'old writings' would make Ignatius call the Old Testament antiquated, which 'is not at all the language which meets us elsewhere in the Ignatian Epistles'.
b: Lightfoot hears 'a slight tinge of depreciation' in pragmasin: it 'points to the vexatiousness of the ordinances of Judaism'. He adds that 'the interchange of γράμμα and πρᾶγμα with scribes and critics is frequent'.

a: in which every tongue that believed in God was gathered together
p: The Syriac, which Lake follows, has 'in which'; the Greek and Latin 'as'; the long recension and Armenian 'into whom'.

readings.w: Lake's text: the Syriac (S) (Lake's footnote); Lightfoot
readings.en: in which every tongue
readings.plain: in which every tongue that believed in God was gathered together

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G) and the Latin (L)
readings.en: as every tongue
readings.plain: just as every tongue that believed in God was gathered together

readings.w: The long recension (g), and the Armenian (A) (Lake's footnote); Zahn
readings.en: into which (or whom) every tongue
readings.plain: into which every tongue that believed was gathered together to God

why: Lake prints the Syriac's reading. Lightfoot: 'This correction of the existing Greek text ὡς is required by the sense and justified by the authorities'; he regards Zahn's eis hon as the long recension's paraphrase.
b: Lightfoot takes hō with 'believed': 'every tongue that believed in it (Christianity) was gathered to God'. Lake's English, followed here, takes it with 'gathered': 'every tongue believing on God was brought together in it'.

a: as Jesus Christ was to the Father
p: The Greek manuscript and the Latin add 'according to the flesh'.

readings.w: Lake's text: the Armenian (A) and the long recension (g) (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: as Jesus Christ to the Father
readings.plain: as Jesus Christ was to the Father

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G) and the Latin (L)
readings.orig: ὡς Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς τῷ πατρὶ κατὰ σάρκα
readings.en: as Jesus Christ to the Father according to the flesh
readings.plain: as Jesus Christ was to the Father in the flesh

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The added words limit Christ's subjection to his human life, which may be why a copyist added them.

a: to Christ and to the Father
p: The Greek manuscript and the Latin add 'and to the Spirit'.

readings.w: Lake's text: the Armenian (A) (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: to Christ and to the Father
readings.plain: to Christ and to the Father

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G) and the Latin (L)
readings.orig: τῷ Χριστῷ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι
readings.en: to Christ and to the Father and to the Spirit
readings.plain: to Christ and to the Father and to the Spirit

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The addition makes the line threefold, like 13:1; Lake prints the shorter form of the Armenian.

a: I have urged you only briefly
p: Two nearly synonymous verbs; Lightfoot prefers the long recension's.

readings.w: Lake's text (G)
readings.en: briefly I urged you
readings.plain: I have urged you only briefly

readings.w: The long recension (g), adopted by Lightfoot (Lake's footnote)
readings.en: briefly I exhorted you
readings.plain: I have encouraged you only briefly

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. Lightfoot adopts parekalesa 'on the ground that it is a common Ignatian word, while παρακελεύειν is not found elsewhere in the Epistles'. The sense hardly changes.

t: 'Through your church' or 'through your fervent prayer'
p: Lightfoot follows the Armenian: the church in Syria is to be refreshed 'through your fervent prayer'.

readings.w: Lake's text (G L)
readings.en: through your church to be bedewed

readings.w: The Armenian (A), followed by Lightfoot (Lake's footnote; Lightfoot's text)
readings.en: through your fervency to be bedewed

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake. Lightfoot's text reads ektenia, 'fervency, urgency', which suits the prayer just asked for; but the Greek manuscript and the Latin agree on 'church', and 'church' is said three times in the verse in Ignatius's manner.
b: Lake's footnote stands at 'church' (Lake's printed page) and gives Lightfoot's reading as 'of your fervent supplication'.

a: they have refreshed me in every way
p: The long recension reads 'you refreshed me', making the Magnesians the subject.

readings.w: Lake's text; the Greek manuscript, the Latin and the Armenian (G L A, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: who refreshed me in every way
readings.plain: they have refreshed me in every way

readings.w: The long recension (g, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: you refreshed me in every way
readings.plain: you have refreshed me in every way

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Greek manuscript and the versions, and Lake's English in making the Ephesians the subject, reading the relative as hoi, 'who', as Lightfoot prints it.
b: The subject is still argued with the better reading. Lightfoot takes 'as you are too' to mean the Magnesians 'were present in the persons of their representatives' (2:1), and 'together with Polycarp' as 'perhaps better taken with' 'greet you' than with 'refreshed me', comparing Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1. On his reading the Ephesians greet the Magnesians together with Polycarp, and those who refreshed Ignatius may include the Magnesian delegates.

p: The Greek manuscript drops the first letter: diakriton, 'divided', for adiakriton, 'unwavering'.

readings.w: Lake's text; the long recension, the Latin and the Armenian (g L A, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: an unwavering (or undivided) spirit

readings.w: The Greek manuscript (G, Lightfoot's apparatus)
readings.en: a divided (or wavering) spirit

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake and all the other witnesses. The Greek manuscript's word gives the opposite of the sense the wish needs, and Lake prints adiakriton without a note.
